notes.meaning: God tells Joshua to put away all fear and discouragement and lead the full army up against Ai. Now that the sin of Achan has been judged and removed, the Lord renews His presence and promises complete victory over the city. When sin is cleared away, God's people can step forward in fresh confidence.

God commands Joshua to destroy Ai and its king just as Israel did to Jericho, but with one major difference: this time the people are allowed to keep the livestock and plunder for themselves. The Lord also directs them to lay an ambush behind the city rather than rely on a frontal assault. This shows that God sometimes uses human planning and military strategy to carry out His work.

Joshua obeys God's instructions by mobilizing the army to march against Ai. He picks a special force of thirty thousand brave warriors and sends them out under the cover of darkness. Moving at night allows them to get into position behind the city without being seen.

Joshua gives strict instructions to the troops sent in secret. They are to hide close behind the town on its west side and remain completely alert. Their success depends on being ready to spring into action the moment they receive the command.

Joshua explains his plan to march toward the town with the main body of soldiers. When the defenders come out to attack just as they did in the first battle, Joshua and his men will turn and run. This intentional retreat is designed to bait the defenders away from their defenses.

Joshua anticipates that the men of Ai will think Israel is panicking just as before, prompting them to leave the city to give chase. By running away, Israel will lure the entire enemy army far from their walls. The overconfidence of Ai will become the very trap that ruins them.

Joshua tells the hidden soldiers that once the enemy has gone, they must rise up and capture the empty town. He reassures them that the Lord their God will hand the city directly to them. Even with careful military strategy, victory rests entirely on God's promise.

Joshua orders the ambush group to set fire to parts of the town as soon as they take it. This fire will serve as a smoke signal to show that the city has fallen. He emphasizes that they are carrying out the explicit command of the Lord.

Joshua sends the ambushers out to wait between Bethel and Ai on the western side of the town. Meanwhile, Joshua stays the night with the main camp of the army. He remains close to the people to encourage them and prepare them for the morning battle.

Joshua rises early in the morning to inspect and organize the troops. He and the elders of Israel then march at the head of the army toward Ai. Having the leaders out front reassures the soldiers and maintains godly order during the campaign.

The main army marches up in plain sight and makes camp on the north side of Ai. A valley lies between the Israelite camp and the walls of the city. This position makes their presence obvious so the king of Ai will see them and take the bait.

Joshua places five thousand men in hiding to the west of the city, between Bethel and Ai. This group forms an ambush close to the walls to strike quickly once the defenders leave. They are positioned where the rugged ground conceals them from view.

With the main army stationed to the north and the rear guard in hiding to the west, all the forces are in position. During the night, Joshua moves down into the valley. He places himself where he can oversee the front line and draw the enemy's attention at daybreak.

Early in the morning, the king of Ai spots the Israelites and rushes out with his troops to fight them at the valley slope. Eager to repeat his earlier triumph, he acts hastily and with reckless confidence. He does not know that an ambush is waiting silently behind his city.

Joshua and the Israelite soldiers pretend to be overwhelmed and flee toward the wilderness. This feigned panic mirrors their genuine defeat from days before. By pretending weakness, Israel tricks the enemy into dropping their guard.

All the fighting men in Ai are called out to chase down the fleeing Israelites. In their excitement to destroy Israel, they pursue Joshua far away from the town. Their desire to wipe out the enemy leads them straight away from their own stronghold.

Every warrior in Ai and neighbouring Bethel joins the chase, leaving their town wide open and unguarded. The allied troops from Bethel had gathered to help Ai and were caught up in the same rush. By leaving the gates open, they leave their homes completely defenceless.

The Lord tells Joshua to stretch out his battle lance toward Ai as the sign that God is handing the city over. Joshua raises his weapon high in obedience. This act gives the visual signal to the hidden troops and reminds Israel that the Lord is fighting for them.

As soon as Joshua raises his lance, the hidden men jump out of their hiding places and charge into Ai. Finding the gates open and the city empty of soldiers, they take it without resistance and immediately set buildings on fire. The rising smoke announces that the first stage of the battle is won.

The men of Ai glance behind them and see thick smoke rising high into the sky. Panic strikes them because they have no way to escape forward or backward. At that exact moment, the Israelites who had been pretending to flee turn around to fight.

When Joshua and the main army see the smoke rising from the city, they know the ambush has succeeded. They halt their retreat, turn around, and attack the pursuers with full force. The hunters suddenly find themselves hunted.

The Israelites who set the city on fire march out of the gates to attack the enemy from behind. The soldiers of Ai are trapped between two forces and cut down completely. Not a single fighter escapes the surrounding ring of Israelite troops.

The king of Ai is captured alive on the battlefield and brought directly to Joshua. He is spared during the heat of combat so that he can face a formal execution. His capture marks the total defeat of his royal leadership.

After slaying all the warriors in the open country and wilderness, the Israelite soldiers march back into Ai itself. They put the remaining population to the sword in full obedience to God's decree of judgment. Israel serves here as the instrument carrying out divine justice on a corrupt city.

A total of twelve thousand men and women fall that day, representing all the people of Ai. The relatively small population explains why Israel had originally thought only a few soldiers were needed to take it. The judgment falls completely on the entire community.

Joshua keeps his arm and lance stretched out until the entire city is devoted to destruction. This steadfast posture recalls Moses holding up his staff until the Amalekites were defeated in Exodus. It serves as an ongoing sign that victory belongs to God and requires steady obedience until the end.

Israel takes the livestock and household goods of the city for themselves, exactly as the Lord had authorized. Unlike Jericho, where all goods were devoted to God alone, Ai's property is given to the people as lawful plunder. God provides for His people's needs when they follow His commands.

Joshua burns the entire town of Ai and reduces it to a permanent mound of ruins. The name Ai literally means 'ruin', and the devastated site remained empty for generations as a lasting memorial. It stood as a silent warning of what happens to nations that resist the living God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern archaeologists note that excavations at et-Tell show no city existed there during the Late Bronze Age, leading some to argue the account is a legendary tale told to explain an ancient ruin, while others suggest Ai was located at a different site such as Khirbet el-Maqatir.

notes.meaning: Joshua executes the king of Ai and hangs his body on a tree until evening. At sunset, obeying the law of Moses, he orders the body taken down and buried under a large mound of stones at the city gate. This public punishment highlights the severe judgment resting upon Canaanite rulers who led their people in rebellion against God.

After the victory at Ai, Joshua leads Israel north to Mount Ebal to build an altar to the Lord. With the central hill country opened up, Israel pauses their campaign to worship God before conquering more land. Putting God's honour first is more important than rushing into the next battle.

Joshua constructs the altar out of uncut stones without using iron tools, following the exact rules Moses gave in the law. On this altar the people present burnt offerings to express total devotion and peace offerings to celebrate fellowship with God. Worship must be offered on God's terms rather than through human invention.

Before all the people, Joshua writes a copy of the law of Moses onto stones coated with plaster. This public inscription places God's standards on open display in the heart of the Promised Land. It reminds everyone of the rules and promises that govern their life as God's nation.

The entire nation divides into two groups, half standing before Mount Gerizim and half before Mount Ebal, with the ark and the priests in the valley between them. Leaders, citizens, and resident foreigners all take their assigned places as Moses had directed. Every member of the community stands together under the authority of God's covenant.

Joshua reads aloud every single word of the law, including the blessings for obedience and the curses for disobedience. The natural shape of the valley between the two mountains allows his voice to carry to the whole crowd. The people hear clearly the serious consequences of walking with God or turning away.

Joshua does not omit a single command that Moses had delivered, reading everything before men, women, children, and resident foreigners. God's word is meant for the entire family and everyone who chooses to join His people. Early and regular exposure to God's truth trains every generation to revere Him.
